utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Thursday, February 5th, 2009. Good morning to Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Praljak, and Mr. Pusic. Good morning to all the Defence counsel. Good morning to Mr. Scott, and his colleague as well as everybody else assisting us. First of all, I'd like to give the floor to Mr. Coric's Defence counsel. Mr. Coric is not present today. The Chamber would like to know why Mr. Coric is absent today. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This morning I received two messages one in writing from Mr. Coric. He wrote to me in these messages that this morning he refused to sign a waiver of his right to be present during the proceedings; and in the second message he asks me to read the letter he addressed in public session, so I'm asking for your permission to read his letter because in it he explains the reasons for his absence. Dear Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic, I'm asking you and all the others who are in any way involved these proceedings whether there can be a just verdict regardless of what it is if it will take almost eight years. I remember one statement by Honourable Judge Antonetti who once said that if everyone acted professionally in the courtroom, then this trial would be completed in three months. I apologise to Mr. President if I misinterpreted his statement. In this connection, I wonder whether three years were not enough for this trial to be nearing the end, if not completed already. I remind you that I intervened in the courtroom once because several months were lost due to the fact that some thousands of pages were not translated. Also, hours and hours are wasted in testimony over discussions whether a Defence team will get several more minutes for their cross-examination or not. Recently, I was a witness to the demonstrative walkout of the Prosecutor from the courtroom. Does this merit even a mild condemnation? I wonder if all the parties are really equal in the courtroom. Did we get an answer to the complaint against the interpreter who grossly insulted the accused during the trial? There are some who in a two-faced manner complain against lack of time and then the Prosecutor's request for additional time is granted. I remind you that dozens of times we discussed the lengthiness of this trial. I'm convinced that you are among those who have done their best for this trial to be over as soon as possible. Regrettably, we are definitively on a good way to set a record for the length of trial. I wonder if this fact does honour to those who have contributed to this development in any way. Watching all this for years, I'm fighting a losing battle for my health, and unfortunately, today I am no longer able to participate in the trial until further notice; that's why I decided to stop taking my pills, the pills that help me go through with this for months and for years. In addition, as part of my personal protest against the way this trial is conducted and how long it is taking, I will refuse all medical assistance regardless of consequences. At this time, I'm not able to participate in the proceedings any further. Dear Ms. Tomasegovic, my power of attorney remains vested in you and Mr. Plavec, but I also demands that you ask for a continuance of the trial until I'm able to return. Thank you for your successful cooperation hitherto, and I congratulate you on your performance in the proceedings. It was misinterpreted, Mr. Coric is asking for a stay of the trial until he is able to return to the courtroom. I thank you for your cooperation hitherto; and I congratulate you on your performance in the proceedings. Respectfully to you and Mr. Plavec. Valentin. Den Haag, 4th February 2009. Your Honours, at this time I have to abide by the wishes of my client and his instructions and ask for the stay -- for a stay of the trial until he returns. I know I have no other details than what I read in the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, about the stay of the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Mr. President each of Your Honours, counsel, all those in and around the courtroom. Well, this certainly comes as much as a surprise to me as it does to everyone else. As I understand what counsel has just said, there is no waiver from Mr. Coric about being absent from the proceedings. And I suppose that raises the question of whether the proceedings can then go forward without the Chamber perhaps - and I'm saying again I'm surprised. I don't have any particular law in front of me at the moment- whether there's particular findings that the Chamber may be able to make in particular circumstances that would allow the trial to go forward in his absence; but I think probably all us, well, I won't speak for everyone but myself, I would have to certainly look into the law further before I could say anything more than that, to be perfectly transparent. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the other Defence counsel want to intervene, otherwise the Judges are going to confer right away. Okay. So we are going to interrupt our proceedings for a few moments and we will deliberate and we'll get back to you with a decision. --- Break taken at 9.09 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Further to its deliberations on the issue raised by the letter of Mr. Coric, letter in which he complains about the duration of the proceedings and in which he informed us that he has decided to stop taking the medication prescribed to him by a medical doctor, and in which he asks for a stay in the proceedings, the Trial Chamber has taken note of what he says in his letter. Moreover, the Trial Chamber indicates that this is a multi-accused trial, that the other accused are also entitled to an expeditious trial; and, therefore, the Trial Chamber indicates that it cannot stay the proceedings. Moreover, Mr. Coric has indicated that he trusts his Defence counsel, and therefore his Defence counsel can, according to the case law deriving from the Chamber's as well as from the Appeals Chamber, his Defence counsel can therefore represent him while he is temporarily absent. In conclusion, the Trial Chamber will continue hearing the witness. We will start with the cross-examination to be carried out by the Prosecution. We also invite the Defence counsel to visit Mr. Coric as soon as possible at the detention centre so that she can take stock of the situation with the accused. The Trial Chamber immediately instructed the legal officer to refer this matter to the chief medical officer of the detention centre so that he can have a look at the situation from a medical standpoint, and so that any necessary measure is taken as far as the health of Mr. Coric is concerned. The Chamber contemplates the possibility of having an ex parte hearing next week with Mr. Coric, his Defence counsel, and the Chamber, again to take stock of the situation. This is the oral decision issued by the Trial Chamber today on the request referred to it. Mr. Praljak you are on your feet. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning to everyone else. I have a few points. I support the position of Mr. Coric. Your decision is your decision, but I wish to say I support him in his position because it's not only about the duration of the trial, it's about a series of other problems that he indicated in his letter. I also had some problems regarding my right to cross-examine which is a challenged every time anew. An enormous number of decisions taken by outvoting within the Trial Chamber, but on the other hand, the Judges find it easy to agree on the most banal things. And some other things that I requested before like how to introduce witnesses, I still have no answer to that; but I believe that there must be a way that some points should be raised in the courtroom. Some points to which everyone has the right. You said that you were surprised, all of us were surprised; but I was not, and I don't want to be included in this without my consent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your position has now been recorded in the transcript. Mr. Stojic. THE ACCUSED STOJIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I fully support my colleague Mr. Coric and Mr. Praljak in everything they said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stojic. It's recorded in the transcript as well. We are going to ask Mr. Usher to bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. You had to wait for 20 minutes, but we had a procedural issue to solve due to the absence of Mr. Coric. The cross-examination will start with Mr. Scott. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Again, good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bozic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And we see each other again.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nice to see you again after five and a half years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, as you perhaps heard at the end of the day yesterday, I have tried - I'll just tell you as I'm telling you I'm also telling the Chamber - I've tried to go back through my own notes and be as efficient as possible not covering ground that's been, at least in my view, adequately covered, but there are few bits and pieces of things that I would like to go back to before moving on to a few more -- some topics in more depth. Just in terms of your background, sir. You mentioned in passing, I think, yesterday that you had performed a period of compulsory military service with the JNA, and can you confirm to us, please, that that service was performed between approximately the spring of 1975 and the end of the winter 1976.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you performed that service, I think, on the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And my understanding is that service involved particular training and assignment in reconnaissance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all right, I said that I as a young boy I was a boy scout, and in the army I practically belonged to that kind of units that were called, I don't remember any long scouts or reconnaissance or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us when you left your period of service at the end of the winter 1976, did you leave the JNA at that time with any particular rank?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have a rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, is it correct that you have dual citizenship, that is in Bosnia-Herzegovina and also in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I have citizenship of Bosnia-Herzegovina and citizenship of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us, please, sir, approximately when did you obtain Croatian citizenship?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly when, but I can say it was roughly at the time when the constitution, or rather, the current legislation of the Republic of Croatia governing citizenship issues made it possible to have dual citizenship, or rather, the obtaining of Croatian citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir -- can you assist us, was it during the period approximately 1992 to 1994, sometime during that period?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember precisely whether it was in that period. If it's important, I can check and tell you later. I can call my wife this evening and ask her to look it up in my passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I'm just asking you to assist as much as you can sir, if you can give us any sort of a time estimate on that. And I guess my final question on that point then for now, do you recall where you made your application for Croatian citizenship; did you go to Zagreb; did you do it somewhere in the Herzegovina region, or how was that done?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour I object on the grounds of relevancy. Why is this line of questioning relevant? Especially yesterday since the gentleman indicated he needed extra time to prepare. Whether he has dual citizenship or not, carries two passports, especially when many others in Bosnia-Herzegovina were doing it irrespective of their ethnic origin. Why is this relevant for this particular witness based on the direct examination and cross of the other parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's come up with a number of witnesses. The Chamber may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's come up with a number of Defence witnesses, spent considerable time talking about the concept of joint citizenship, what that meant, the ramifications for whether one had refugee status, the moment of people, et cetera, certain advantages flowing from having dual citizenship. I might agree with Mr. Karnavas if I spent 15 or 20 or 30 minutes on the topic. I've asked two or three questions, and I think this is my last question. I do think, however it's relevant overall to this man's backgrounds and character.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well go ahead then. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my last question on this topic is a very simple one, can you recall where you applied for Croatian citizenship? If you can't recall the particular time-period then can you remember where you made your application?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think I applied at the consulate in Mostar. I'm not sure, but I think it was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, going back to your positions and your roles at the Department of Defence, and if you allow me sir, probably in the course of the cross-examination, I will probably refer to it as the Department of Defence. Everyone in the courtroom is aware of the fact that sometime in the latter part of the 1993 the terminology may have changed to ministry, although I think you established in your testimony with Ms. Alaburic that that was primarily a matter of change of names more than anything else. If you'll forgive me I'm just going to use the term "Department of Defence". Is it correct, sir, that during the time that you held the position of deputy minister, you were the only senior official at the Department of Defence to hold the title "deputy" as opposed to assistant minister?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the decision about the basic organisation of the Defence Department and later the decision on the organisation of the Defence Department, it was stipulated precisely who held which position and who was in charge of which affairs; and from both documents, it was obvious that there was a position of the deputy and a certain number of assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The answer to my question, sir, was yes, you were the only one who had the position deputy?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I confirm precisely what is written in the decision on the basic organisation and the decision on the organisation of the Defence Department governing various positions within the department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And your direct superior at all times, at least during this period from approximately August of 1992 to at least November of 1993, your immediate superior was Mr. Stojic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just to be clear on that, there were no -- there was no other level of management, if you will. There was no one between you and Mr. Stojic? You reported to and took direction from directly Mr. Stojic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not exactly the way it was. It's not exactly the way you had put it. In fact, I was Mr. Stojic's deputy whose line of work was perfectly clear within the civilian sector of the Defence Department, and that in part Mr. Stojic gave me orders and -- or instructions, and that is the area in which I reported to Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There was no other management level between you and Mr. Stojic? It's a very simple question, sir. Did you have some other superior that supervised your work and that you reported to other than Mr. Stojic? It's a very simple question, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the answer was very simple too. I reported to Mr. Stojic for my own line of work as the person who was in charge of civilian affairs within the Defence Department, and that is the work that was carried out by the deputy head of the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct, sir, that your role involved, as deputy, acting as the replacement or substitute for Mr. Stojic when authorised to do so?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Practically I could not stand in for Mr. Stojic, although the position I held was called the deputy head of the Defence Department for a simple reason; Mr. Stojic was a member of the HVO HZ-HB as the collective temporary executive organ in the area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and as such, he had been chosen by the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I stood in for Mr. Stojic only at certain sessions of the HVO of the Croatian communities of Herceg-Bosna, as I've already said during my previous testimony. And this happened when I was a rapporteur with regard to certain matters at sessions of the HVO HZ-HB and also on certain occasions when due to certain private commitments Mr. Stojic was not in a position to attend these session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question wasn't limited to simple substituting for Mr. Stojic at the meetings of the HVO HZ-HB, but more generally. If there were occasions if other officials came to the Department of Defence for some other reason if there were other functions going on at the Department of Defence, and Mr. Stojic for one reason or another was not available, you stood in for him on a number of occasions; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. That was not my function to stand in for Mr. Stojic. I as a lawyer, and you too, and Their Honours look at regulations and how things are regulated in the rules. I held this function which was the function of deputy head of the Defence Department, and within that I had my specific line of work that I carried out. Not in a single document does it say or is there any mention of this that within my line of work, I also stand in for Mr. Stojic when he is not present within the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One question. This concerns my understanding regarding his belonging to the HVO. You said that as the deputy of Mr. Stojic, you represented Mr. Stojic during the HVO meetings when he was not there. So my question generally, I'm not saying that the HVO is a government, but I was thinking about the level of organisation. In a government, deputy ministers are also members of the government, and if you as a deputy, if you were not a member, does that mean that the people sitting in the HVO were chosen into a t-personee [phoen], meaning based on their personal qualities and not based on their assignments? Were there, in this case, deputies who were members at the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Mindua, I wish to explain to you that deputies of the head of the Defence Department were not members of this government, that is the HVO HZ-HB. It was only the heads who were members of the government, and they were elected by the legislative body that at that time was the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I was not a member of the government. I've already said this twice over the past three days, if not even more often, that I was present at government meetings when certain documents were being proposed. And I was the person sponsoring the proposal of the Defence Department, but I did not attend these sessions as a member of the government; and I did not have the authority that the members of government had, and persons who were elected members of government. I'm saying this in a figurative sense. When I say government, it was the HVO HZ-HB, and it was consisted of the elected representatives of the Defence Department, elected by the legislative legal body. I as the deputy head of the Defence Department - as I've already said in my previous statements - was not elected by that legislative legal body. I was elected by that same government, the HVO HZ-HB. I was elected a deputy carrying out a certain line of work but who was not a member of that same government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Witness, let me take a clear example so that we understand because it's rather difficult and complex. Here is my example: Let us take the case of Mr. Stojic who would, let's say, be held at a check-point, and he is not allowed to go through. His Motorola is confiscated and he is, between inverted commas, a prisoner; he is not allowed to do anything. You are in the building, in the office next to his secretary's office, and all of a sudden, municipality or brigade sends a logistic request for a doctor or for a truck. Mr. Stojic, well, you cannot get a hold of Mr. Stojic. Who would take a decision in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, that's a very good question. It shows that there weren't proper regulations in force that would say who would regulate the matter. I did not have the authority to do that. My authority is in line with regulations and rules in that field, and that is in the Defence Department, and only has to do with the civilian sector. That is a confirmation, perhaps, which I can understand as a lawyer, and you as lawyers will understand me better when I say that this is this lack of regulation. It only confirms a particular thesis, how temporary or provisional this type of government was. Many things had not been regulated. Many things that only later when the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was established towards the end of 1993 were being resolved or an attempt was made to resolve them, although I believe that that was a provisional authority, although it was called the government of Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. So in this specific case, I did not have the powers to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I take note of what you have just said. I will now use another example, a second concrete example. I do not know whether in Bosnia and Herzegovina if there are earthquakes in this area, but let us just imagine that in a given area there is an earthquake with buildings destroyed and civilians hurt. And the president of the municipality asks for help and makes a request to the Department of Defence, so that the Department of Defence sends the necessary means to help the people in the rumbles and sends a logistic means of food, et cetera. Let's imagine Mr. Stojic is also under the rumbles. Who in the Defence Department in such a situation would give the necessary instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all right. I mean, it's a hypothetical situation, isn't it; and I am willing to accept it as an example in terms of who would make a decision to involve all the military and the logistics in this. My logical answer to that would be that it would be the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as the supreme commander who can decide to have the army used in such situations. However, in order to be of assistance to you, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, this was a very good example that you referred to in case of a natural disaster, that is. Within the civilian sector, it was envisaged that -- well, this was a sector that was supposed to belong to the sector that I headed theoretically and that was civilian protection. That has to do with natural disasters. This particular division never started functioning within the Defence Department, and I know that there was this big debate between the Ministry of the Interior, rather the department of the interior and the Defence Department who would take care of this particular work. And finally it went to a place where it didn't belong, and that was the Department of the Interior. So I'm trying to explain to you the actual situation as it was, and the regulations that were there in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just in the same course of questions, when asked by Mr. Scott, Mr. Bozic, you were deputy head of the department, you answered in the affirmative. What does that mean? Is it nothing but an empty label, or does it have any meaning at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for this question, Your Honour Judge Trechsel, you put it very well. Was this in a name only, this particular position. First of all, I was not a creator. I do not know how President Boban proposed the establishment as such. However, this particular position, deputy head of the Defence Department was specifically linked to a line of work that is called the sector for civilian affairs. In order to make things easier for you - I mean to understand the entire situation - towards the end of December 1993, when the ministry was formed, the Ministry of Defence of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, then the deputy minister became exactly the embodiment of what you asked me about and what Mr. Scott asked me about, that this links up all sectors within the Ministry of Defence as such. Within that structure of the Ministry of Defence, that is to say, from mid-December 1993, the work that I carried out as the deputy was now subdivided between two assistants: The assistant between personnel matters and supplies, which is what I talked about on the first day. That for awhile I carried out that particular work as well parallel with my function of the head of the office for contacts with UNPROFOR and international organisations. And the other part of my work was carried out by another assistant, and that also had to do with mobilisation and things like that. So this shows how this function of deputy head of the Defence Department, and someone made decisions to that effect, and I cannot explain why. Formally I did have the function of deputy head, but in the very next line, my function is limited by the fact that I'm responsible for and in charge of part of the work within the civilian affairs section of the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In other words, you could have said, Yes practically it's just a name. And I would really invite you to try to make short answers. Thank you. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, throughout the course of your -- the cross-examination there may come times when I will refer you back to your -- the interview that you gave over a period of days in November of 2003. And, sir, at that time you did confirm that you did act as a replacement for Mr. Stojic; and you did, for example, indicate that you received dignitaries and visitors to the ministry or Department of Defence on Mr. Stojic's behalf when he was not available. That is what is you said in November 2003, have you changed your position since then?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Perhaps when my learned friend puts the interview to the witness, it would be useful to get the actual reference and to perhaps quote the line if it's not too long. It will be easier to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In that particular instance the two in the part one of his interview on page 27, and again in part one of his interview at page 41.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, is this interview in the binder because we were not -- we had not heard about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it is marked fork the record purposes P 10796, 794. My apology, P 10794.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's in binder 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Binder 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: While His Honour is looking at that sir, let me persist at my question with -- I hope I've been able to assist counsel in court. Sir, that is's what you said in 2003. Are you changing your answers in what you are conveying to the Judges of this Court?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I have a look at my statement, the one that you are referring to, the one that's in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this question -- let's make it more concrete based on something that you've said in the last couple of days. When you were being questioned about the 9th of May, 1993, the events in Mostar on that day, you were called by SpaBat because their APCs had been blocked on the entrance to Mostar. You then apparently intervened on that situation. You called the duty officer to deal with that situation. You then told Judge Trechsel that after that particular intervention, you apparently rolled over and went back to sleep. Later that day, you -- later that morning, you then did contact Mr. Stojic, and as part of your answer, apparently in why you had not called Mr. Stojic earlier, you said on a number of -- in a number of situations, you sought to resolve those matters yourself by delegation or otherwise and not to - if you will - bother Mr. Stojic if not necessary. So now, sir, what authority were you exercising when you delegated authority to resolve certain situations instead of bothering Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do ask, I do apologise for interrupting my learned friend. I am looking firstly at page 27 of the interview that my learned friend cited, and I don't - I must be missing something - but I don't actually see the line that supports the question. What I do see is at line 13 a question from my learned friend: "During the time that you were deputy minister of defence, did you attend any meetings any part of the Republic of Croatia?" And the answer was no. So I don't see from page 27 anything that supports the question. Your Honour, I do think if my learned friend is going to spend any time on this interview, the appropriate course is as the witness requested, that he be given access to this interview that he took part in, and he can look at the context and we can all follow it. I'm asking for verbatim quotes if my learned friend is putting proposition to the witness. Your Honour, of course, the witness also held different positions which he has described both as a deputy minister of defence and something completely different when he was working with UNPROFOR. So I think it will be useful to Your Honours and to us to follow the evidence if my learned friends is specific and quotes the interview line by line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, what is the line where he says that he replaced Mr. Stojic which would be in contradiction with what he is saying just now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Page 27 and Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please for Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Apologies. The portion of the version I have of the transcript, Your Honour, doesn't have line numbers, but towards top of the page Mr. Bozic says halfway through the first paragraph signed by him: "And who was replacing or acting on behalf of the Defence Department when he, the representative, authorised me to represent him." That's what I'm referring to in that particular instance specifically. And I also referred, Your Honours to another instance on page 41 when he talks about receiving visitors on Mr. Stojic's behalf. Let me go back, sir, I have a pending question for you unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I do not agree with what you said because looking at the English version, you asked the question and Mr. Bozic answered, and I quote: "I was not the second person. I was the deputy who was in charge of the civilian part." So his answer is not as affirmative as you indicated. I refer everybody to this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, with great respect, Your Honour, you are stopping too soon. You are stopping at: "... civilian aspect, and who was replacing or acting on behalf of the representative of the Defence Department when he the representative authorised me to represent him." That's also in the transcript. If I can go back to the other specific scenario.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but in legal terms he said when he was authorised to represent him. This is what he said. He did not say that he was -- he had the permanent authorisation to do so, he said that he needed to have an authorisation to represent him. This is what he said. Mr. Witness, this is the answer you gave a few years ago. Since you are a lawyer, I believe that when you mention that, you were giving also a legal answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to ask you something first and foremost. I'm not trying to evade any answer, and I'm going to answer all questions that are put to me. It is a fact that Mr. Scott, during these talks that we conducted over five and a half years, promised me to submit a transcript of this conversation in the Croatian language; and he hasn't done this in the past five and a half years. And I cannot deal with without reading my statement, reading what I had said. I will give Your Honours comments with regard to everything I stated, but I ask that I have the transcript before me in the Croatian language so that I can give reliable answers to these questions. I mean, for me to go back five and a half years, and it depends on how people read things; and as I listen to what you've been saying, I see that you understand certain things differently from the way Mr. Scott understands them, and this is not very pleasant for me. So therefore, I kindly ask could I please have the transcript in Croatian, and then I'm going to give answers to all questions put to me. Until then, I do not feel capable of going back five and a half years in time and recalling everything that I discussed over three exhausting days with Mr. Scott with hundreds of questions, sub-questions, going back to one in the same thing with yet new questions. So you are asking me to deal with this now. I said that I am, as you've said, a witness for justice, and in order to be one, I need to have the document that I can read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fair enough. Since we do not have the B/C/S text, that will be very difficult. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will confirm, I will do this to the extent I will confirm that there is no B/C/S transcript of this. It was provided, the original audio recording has been provided to the Defence in both languages. Just to answer the Judge's questions and it is one of the problems, frankly, when there is a long series questions of interventions after the Prosecution puts a question, way back now when this whole -- when I first put these question to the witness back on page 12, line 3. "And is it correct, sir, that your role involved as deputy acting as a replacement or substitute for Mr. Stojic when authorised to do so?" That is the question I've been pursuing now for the last 20 minutes or so, 25 minutes or so since the question was first put. So that is exactly the point. And that relates back to the prior testimony. So had there not been a long series of inventions and long answers by the witness, there would have been a stronger connection to the original question. If I can go back --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just say, I do apologise sincerely for interrupting Mr. Scott. I do have the page 27 now. One of the difficulties I've found if one looks, there are a number of interviews under this tab number. And I was looking at the wrong page 27. I think that's just something to be aware of as we go forward. But, Your Honour, I would ask if we don't have the B/C/S version of this interview that it's only fair in the normal practice that if a previous statement is being put to the witness, he is entitled to see it. It would have been far preferable in my submission to get this transcript translated if my learned friend for the Prosecution was seeking to put it to the witness in the box today. Your Honour, be that as it may, and without prejudice to any further submissions I may make on that issue, at the very least what I do ask Your Honours to do is to require Mr. Scott - if he is not otherwise willing to do it - to read out verbatim the answers when he puts questions to the witness as far as they relate to the interview that took place some years ago. I think that's only fair, and it is only proper. I do apologise for interrupting, but it is an important point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, if you go back to any issue that relate to the interviews carried out several years ago, then you will have to read verbatim both the question and the answer. At least we'll be able to read it and hear it in our earphones. Please continue, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will endeavour to do my best. I would hope there might be situations Mr. Bozic will be able to assist us by simply indicating, Yes that's what I said before. If we are going to engage in exercise of reading every prior question and answer to him, we will certainly be here for substantially longer than we otherwise would be. So I hope maybe he can be forthcoming with us on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, there was a question put now some minutes to you, and it's long gone off the transcript page, but let me go back and try again. You testified, sir, that on the 9th of May at one point you had intervened after being called by the Spanish Battalion about being blocked by Mostar. You then called a duty officer to deal with that situation. You then later on said that when asked by, I think, Judge Trechsel why it was you didn't contact Mr. Stojic soon around that time and if that wasn't exactly Judge Trechsel's question, I beg some leeway, but that's certainly my question. In any event that's certainly my question at this time. And you said to the effects that well, there were on various situations you would act about try to solve the problem yourself, that's my para-phrase, you used the term delegation and would not try to bother Mr. Stojic. So what authority, sir, when you were acting in that case to intervene and to delegate and solve problems without disturbing Mr. Stojic, what then authority were you exercising, if not as deputy?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was exercising the authority of a member of the commission for contacts with the UNPROFOR to which I was appointed before being appointed deputy head of the Defence Department, and I was never replaced from that position until the office was elected. And I clarified yesterday that I had done certain things on behalf of the commission, things that regarded not only the department, but other bodies of the HVO HZ-HB, so even that communication on the 9th of May with the Spaniards was part of my job on behalf of the commission for contacts with the UNPROFOR on the part of the HVO HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. We'll come back to that when we get to the 9th of May and we'll see if we can pursue that a little bit further. You remained in this position as deputy minister, deputy head, if you will, before the term minister was used, until approximately November 1993. I want to clarify after that, sir, you then remained in various functions and duties related to the what was then the minister of defence even when you were no longer by title, at least, deputy minister; is that correct? You had some roles related to personnel?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Scott, I really did not understand this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you to go to P 07090 in the binders that you have, and I'll have to be assisted which binder it's in. Binder number 2.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, which number did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: P 07090. Sir, this is a decision to establish the military council of the minister of defence dated 9th of December, 1993, over the name of Mate Boban in the English version. And in that list under section Roman numeral II, it says, the following are here by appointed to the military council as members, and number 5 defence minister's assistant for personnel matters, Slobodan Bozic; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And keeping that in mind, please, can I ask you to next turn to P 08215, also in binder 2. It shouldn't be too far from the one you were just looking at. P 08215. This is a list of employs of the Ministry of Defence --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I haven't found it yet. P?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is a list of Ministry of Defence employees as of the 20th of April, 1994. If you'll find the heading that says personnel administration on page 2 of the English version. Person listed as 1, Slobodan Bozic, assistant minister for personnel. You see that? Can you confirm that, sir? It will assist everyone in the courtroom - you may not wants to assist me - but it will assist the courtroom sir, if some of these answers if you could tell us, isn't it correct, sir that you continued even though you were no longer deputy to Mr. Stojic when he left the department in November 1993, you continued in a senior role in connection with personnel administration throughout 1993 and 1994? Very simple, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do object, I do object. It's completely unnecessary to make these snide comments on the side. There's been no indication from the witness that he is not willing to assist any party in this courtroom, whether it be the Defence or the Prosecution or Your Honours. And, Your Honours, to cast aspersions on a witness without a foundation is really unworthy of a Prosecutor of my learned friend's ability and experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said he is a witness of the court. Therefore it's not necessary to address these issues. He is witness of the court. He has taken the oath, so he will answer these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I try to get into this area again by a simple question without need together resort to the documents. Judge Trechsel already admonished the witness once to give short answers, and I leave the record at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it correct, you look at these two documents, P 07090, P 08215 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, wait. It may be more complicated than you think. Let's go back to this document, Witness. It's dated the 20th of April, 1994. There's another defence minister at the time. This document contains a list of the staff of the Ministry of Defence. Looking at this list, we see that there is an inspection. There is an immediate office for the minister with the chief of the immediate office. There are general administrative services, and there's also a unit called personnel administration. There are 14 staff within that administration, and you were number one because you are numbered as 1. In fact, you are in charge of this administrative unit, and next to it in English, next to your name, your title is indicated, namely assistant minister for personnel; but this reference is also found for your other colleagues. Let's check, for instance, civilian affairs, Mr. Barbaric. His title is also assistant minister. Now, it seems that in the administrative system as it stood at the time, the chief of the administrative units were given the title of assistant ministers. Is that the way things have to be interpreted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I would now like to kindly ask without any intention to waste time because time is important to me as well. I wish to finish as soon as possible after more than 14 days in The Hague, but I have to give answers that are all the truth and nothing but the truth, as my solemn declaration requires me. Mr. Scott deliberately or not, I believe not deliberately, is making a connection between two periods. One period when there was a Defence Department with Mr. Stojic in it. And the second period is the one to which these two documents now shown by Mr. Scott, apply. The documents you discussed. I have to go back to the first day of my evidence when I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Witness, I've asked you a specific question. We are talking about 1994. I'm not mixing things up. I'm a professional, and I'm talking about the specific date of the document. That's why I specify the 20th of April, 1994, and I indicated that it wasn't the same minister. So on the single, on the sole basis of this document, could you please tell me whether the fact that you are number one within this personnel administration unit, whether it meant that, in fact, you were number two of within the Ministry of Defence, or whether, as the other colleagues you had at the time, you were the head of an administrative unit? My question is very specific.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will answer your question very precisely. That referred to one division. But I have to remind you of my evidence given on the first day that I was elected on the 1st December 1993, as head of that commission for contacts with the UNPROFOR, and at the request of Minister Jukic and later Minister Soljic, I remained as acting head of that personnel division. And I was never actually appointed to that position, but I was an acting officer doing simultaneously two jobs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you are saying is that you were the head of the personnel division, but you say that you were acting because, in fact, your job was the person in charge of contacts with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, I've tried to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was, again, I thought abundantly clear to everyone in the courtroom what is happening. Twelve minutes ago, at 4 minutes after 10, I asked the witness this question. Page 25 starting at line 25: "I want to clarify" after that -- no, I'm sorry: "You were deputy minister, if you will, before the term minister was used until approximately November 1993. I want to clarify," to use your words, Mr. President, "I want to clarify after that, sir, you then remained in various functions and duties related to that then to that minister of defence even when you were no longer by title at least deputy minister; is that correct. You had some roles related to personnel." The answer it to that question would have been, Yes. That would have been about you know 14 minutes ago. And that's all I was try together establish. If we could move forward a little bit through the chronology so we could talk about Mr. Bozic's continuing contacts in these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, sir, it's correct, is it not that from the end of 1993 and well into 1994, you continued to have a position, a senior position, if not deputy assistant minister related to personnel matters; correct? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I acted as deputy -- there is assistant minister for personnel affairs, but I never occupied that position, I just did that work temporary at the request of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How long, sir, did you continue doing that work?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first day of my evidence, I said that unfortunately it went on into 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, how long into 1994, sir, approximately? Please help us.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can even suppose that it happened into 1995 because the minister's asked me to stay in that position since heads of the division for personnel and head of division for procurement were appointed and they wanted to keep me as a coordinator.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you very much. You've answered my question. Now, I'd also like to come back to the topic of the location of the offices of Department of Defence, at least what we might call the headquarters office, Mr. Stojic's seat, if you will, that you went through and took us to some extent both with Ms. Nozica and again with Ms. Alaburic. But I want to focus, I want to be very clear about a particular period of time, sir, so let me focus your attention from mid-April 1993 until the end of June 1993. Do you have those dates in mind? Mid-April 1993 until the end of June 1993. Yes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us during that time where the Department of Defence offices, which included both you and Mr. Stojic were located?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, I'd like to intervene. As regards Mr. Coric, I asked for the chief medical officer to visit right away Mr. Coric. I'm being told that the visit will take place tomorrow right away. And this is 19 past 10.00 this very morning. I'm instructing the Registrar to take the necessary measures. Please continue, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I have a pending question to you again already as so often this morning. Can you tell us, please, where that office was located during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the offices were on the premises of the agronomy institute, or to be more precise in the building housing the administration of an agronomy complex called Apro, A-p-r-o, of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you give us, sir, it may assist us in the future, and of course I suspect for you when you say that agronomy institute, you know exactly where that is. Can you give us an approximate street address or intersection in two streets in Mostar, so it will assist the Judge at some point to know exactly where that was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be quite honest, I'm not sure whether it was Kralj Tomislav Street or something else. If I'm looking at the entrance from Siroki Brijeg from which I used to come, then 500 or 700 metres from the Mostar cathedral, that's where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Is it true, sir, that throughout the entire period, now focusing on when you joined the DOD, if you will, in approximately August of 1992 until Mr. Stojic's departure in November 1993, the two of you always had your offices in close proximity to one another?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the office of Mr. Stojic and my office had the secretary's office between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you share that secretary, if you will?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we shared the same secretary. And now I recall that for awhile we had another girl doing secretarial jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In terms of people who officed at this location, and we heard about a number of them yesterday, but let me ask you about one more, do you recall that the man named Mladen Naletilic also known as "Tuta" also had an office close by to Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those offices in that building, I'm no longer sure when we moved in, whether it was the end of August or the beginning of September. I'm not sure whether there was anyone from the units of the Convicts Battalion, which had its offices there. There was one office, even later where the secretaries sat, but I know as a native of Siroki Brijeg, I know that Mr. Tuta had his offices in the tobacco station in Siroki Brijeg, the offices of the Convicts Battalion whereas in our building we had offices occupied most of the time by a young girl.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in terms of your role in personnel administration and in the department, again I would like to touch on a few things which I had hoped we would be able to do rather quickly. But if I can just take you back, please, to Exhibit P 00586. In the first binder, P 00586. This is the decision on the internal organisation or constitution of the Department of Defence, dated 17 October, 1992. I think we've seen it in the courtroom before, perhaps several times. If I can ask you, sir, to look in particular to Roman numeral III, section Roman numeral III, which is in the English version is on page 3. And this is a document that went out apparently over the name of Mr. Stojic, you see on the first page. In Roman numeral III, it says: "The head shall have a deputy full stop. The deputy head is directly responsible for the civilian section, which shall include the following organisational units: " And we can see them all there. I won't read them, except among those you'll see number 5, personnel administration; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can next ask you to go to P 02477, P 02477, also in the first binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Just help me, which part?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry Your Honours. Good morning. I don't understand this comment by Mr. Scott. I don't know if we are looking at the same thing, line 34, that is page 34, line 8, it says "over the name of Mr. Stojic." If we look at the document, this was signed by Mr. Boban. I don't think it's a good idea to leave this on the record. I don't see Mr. Stojic's name on the document. Perhaps I misunderstood my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe counsel, if you look at the first page of P 00 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe, sir, if you'll find -- if I misspoke, I apologise. I was referring to the first page of that document P 00586, distributing, I will correct myself to say the cover letter, if you will, distributing the document by Mr. Boban. Perhaps we are both a little bit right. My apologies if I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you see that and then I also direct your attention to P 02477.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you tell me in which section of the binder is that, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: First binder, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can we have the usher's assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you very much, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you look, sir, at Roman numeral II of that document, which is on the English, the bottom of the first page. This is the decision on the internal organisation of the Defence Department, and it talks about in the second paragraph under Roman numeral II: "Chiefs of administration for Defence affairs and mobilisation, budget administration, civilian protection staff, legal affairs administration, personnel administration, and welfare administration manage the work of those administrations and answer for their work to the deputy head." And that was you, sir; is that correct, the deputy head?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm told, Your Honour, by my colleague that it's perhaps time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are right. We'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I can direct your attention next, please, to 2D 01017 in binder number 2. That will be a Defence exhibit at that. 2D - some of the documents that you were shown by Ms. Nozica - 2D 01017.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, Mr. Scott, the last document that I opened before the break was P 02477. That's what you said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, but we are moving on to another document now.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, where is this other document? Where is this other document?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I beg your pardon, I believe that it would be a good idea that this be explained to the witness, namely how the documents are organised. I think that would be a good idea because I think he cannot find his way in the binder. He doesn't know how the documents are organised, the P documents, the 1D, D documents, and so on. I think it would be good to instruct him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we have two binders. The documents are filed with bearing letters P and figures in the chronological order, and then you have Defence 2D, 3D, et cetera, which is presented in an order which might be different.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fair enough. And in addition, Witness, you can see the document on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, you have that document now --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 2D 01017. Sir, can you just look at that. I'm not going to take you through the document in any detail, but if you can look at that and confirm that these are the rules as stated in the title page. These are the rules on the conditions and procedure for assignment awarding ranks and promotion to higher ranks applicable to the HVO armed forces. And the date of this document is 14th of October, 1992. Do you see that? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And these would have been the rule that is would have within -- that were applicable to those topics during the period of latter part of 1992 and, would it be accurate to say through at least the end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was signed by Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just as an example, and again I'm not going to take your time or the courtroom's time to go through it, but even at the back there were even such things as forms that have to be completed; correct? Information required, for example, to justify promotion, different dates and service records; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you next, please, to go to 2D 00933. Again, sir, you should be able to find that roughly in the same part of the binder. Binder number 2 in the 2D exhibit.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you confirm to us, sir, that this is an order dated the 16th of July, 1993, by Mr. Stojic indicating, or someone over Mr. Stojic's name - so I don't want to get bogged down on whether it's Mr. Stojic's signature or not - but going out over his name and title, an order, 1: "Send proposals for awarding ranks, promotion to higher ranks, and assignment of ranks within seven days." Number 2: "Proposals of officers and non-commissioned officers of all units shall be sent through the Main Staff to the personnel administration of the Defence Department." Et cetera, and would you just confirm for us that that was indeed the procedure for the awarding of ranks, promotion and assignment of ranks as further confirmed by Mr. Stojic as of July 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the procedure for proposals to award ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I could next ask you to go to P 00502. We are going to go back to the first binder, please. Different binder. P 00502. Sir, this appears to be a list of the, I think this may have been shown to you earlier, maybe not, I may be confusing it with another document. But it's dated the 18th of September, 1993, giving kind of a personnel structure, organisations, number of positions for the HVO effective immediately, as I say again over the name of Mr. Stojic. And when I say - let me just say it to counsel - when I say, "over the name of," I'm not trying to get into whether it's actually his signatures or not but on the authority of Mr. Stojic as head of the Department of Defence. And if I can ask you to look at least in the English, I'll try to assist you if I can with the B/C/S. But on page 9 of the English version, but if you'll find in the document there's a section that relates to the personnel section several pages into the chart, if you will, there is a section personnel. It's on page 9 of the English. It may be on page -- there's, unfortunately, no page number on the B/C/S one. I apologise. Item 50 at one point, I think it's item 50 the numbers are consecutive. In any event sir, if you see that, this list the personnel section, a chief, a personnel affairs officer, a labour relations officer, and an operator typist. And if you could just simply confirm for me, sir, that during this period of time, during 1993, this personnel administration or personnel section was rather small operation; is that correct? Four people, five people, six people?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I would like to go back to the first page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my question to you is this: During this time 1993, was the personnel -- did the staffing of the personnel administration, was it generally in the vicinity of four, five, six persons? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This doesn't have anything to do with the personnel department at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Then forgive me if I'm wrong. Forget the document, sir. The personnel administration that you supervised, we looked at the document earlier you agreed that personnel administration was one of your responsibilities as deputy chief. In 1993, how many people worked in that section?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which period of 1993 do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's say the second half of 1993. Let's say from July to December of 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I cannot be very specific, but it's a personnel department consisting of six, seven persons, eight at a maximum. Although, the specific number was established yesterday when we looked at that structure within the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And where were those offices of the personnel administration, the people that these six, seven, or eight persons, where were they physically located? Where did they office in relation to your office?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Near my office on the same floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to turn to the topic of reporting at the Department of Defence, which I'm sure has been discussed to some extent. But is it fair to say, sir, that in the course of being the minister of defence, Mr. Stojic regularly received reports on a whole host of matters including the military situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say that he received quite a few reports regarding the work that his assistants sent reports to him about, and some of the reports probably have to do with the Main Staff as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me show you an example. P 01114. This will be in your first binder. Binder 1, in numerical order, P 01114. You may --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you say that it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Usher, you may have to just take up a chair next to the witness, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would ask if it would be possible for the usher to sit next to me because I really don't want to have all this time go by without me having a look at the documents. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this is an example, I put it to you as an example the kind of reports that I suggest to you, I'm putting to you that Mr. Stojic would have received, did receive on a regular basis. This one being a report dated the 13th of January, 1993 from someone, I believe, named Zeljko Akra [phoen], reporting on the situation in Gornji Vakuf in Novi Travnik at the top of it head of the Defence Department, personally to Mr. B. Stojic. That's at type of report that Mr. Stojic received on a regular basis; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say this is the type of reports that he received, but I cannot say whether it was on a regular basis. I said already that he received in from the Main Staff and other sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, do you think that Mr. Stojic as a minister of defence took prudent steps to keep himself informed about defence matters in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not quite understand your question. What do you mean by necessary steps?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you think, sir, that Mr. Stojic as a minister of defence took prudent steps to keep himself informed about defence matters in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously he did receive information and reports and that could be seen on the basis of what you have shown me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you will turn next, please, to P 02823. P 02823. First binder in numerical order.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, this particular document is a communication dated 17th of June, 1993, from Major-General Praljak. It says to Bruno Stojic, as well as the Main Staff: "URGENT! Inform us ASAP when the tanks are arriving in Rama!" My particular question about this document actually has very little do with that, but there's a stamp on the middle lower middle centre of the document, I guess you might say, that he been added and certain information filled in. For example, to orient you, the first line in the box it says GS HVO, which I think we can agree means the HVO Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, is it fair to say this is what we would call a packet communication?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that was an electronic form of sending a signal, a wireless signal through the air and with a print-out facility at the other end; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although I'm not very knowledgeable about this particular system but I believe that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The box we are looking at here, the one dependent that starts GS HVO, appears to have the number 3468, appears to say 17/06/1993, which I'm going to suggest to you - and I am sure I'll be corrected if I'm wrong - which is 17 June, 1993, which will correspond to the date on the document itself, at 0840, presumably 840 hours, 8.40 a.m. Now, who would put that stamp on an incoming or outgoing if you will, whichever you wants to address it. Who would put that stamp on and complete that information?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said I'm not very knowledgeable about this particular system, but I believe this was done by the operations person who had received the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We can tell since it appears to be coming from Mr. Praljak to the Main Staff the person who received it - again trying to be as clear as possible - this was the duty officer, communications officer at the Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, I'm not very knowledgeable about this system but I assume it was the operations person who was working on these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now if we could look at very quickly some additional reports just in connection to the topic of reports, the type of reports going to Mr. Stojic. Can I ask you to turn next, please, to P 00653. First binder. P 00653.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you can just scan through that document, I'll tell you again I'm not going to take you through any detailed part of it. If you could just scan it if you will, please, enough to see what it is. This says intelligence report number 89/92 for the 26th of October, 1992, on the last page or beneath the name of the intelligence chief, the distribution 1, head of Defence Department, Bruno Stojic personally; number 2, Commander J. Bobetko personally; 3, HVO GS staff brigadier, M. Petkovic personally, et cetera; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And sir, the Judges can under, can't they, and properly so, that again this is the kind of a report that Mr. Stojic and others received on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's an example. I'll not talking about things on a regular basis because I really don't know about that, but this was something that was received from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, looking at the list of beneficiaries, I see the name of General Bobetko. How do you explain that a general from a foreign country should receive a document, an internal document which is internal to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, this is the first time I see this document. I don't know what I could say by way of response except that the person sending this knew what he was doing. Everything else I would say would be speculation, and I really don't want to engage in that. What you said is correct that this was submitted to General Bobetko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it is a packet communications or a transmission by fax, this meant that the Republic of Croatia had a direct connection with the units on field? Is this an assumption? How can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot explain. I really don't know that, and that is why I said that whatever I would say would be speculation. Who sent this knew why he sent it. Now, did he want to raise his document to a higher level or whatever, I really don't know. I really don't know what was meant by this. And I don't know whether there was any kind of packet communication between and among the military structures of the Herceg-Bosna and the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off, we have great difficulty hearing the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you'll turn next to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology. P 02760 in the first binder. Should be, well, not immediately next door, but in that same binder. P 02760.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And this is the last one of these I'll show you. I won't take the time to go through more in the interest of time. That is document dated the 14th of June, 1993. Also from the chief of military intelligence, Mr. Keza. If you will look please again at the distribution below Mr. Keza's name, Herceg-Bosna president, Mate Boban, personally; Bruno Stojic, personally; Mr. Petkovic, personally. I'll stop there for a moment, but I'll follow up on Judge Antonetti's questions in a moment, but can you confirm that much for us? Again this is a military intelligence report concerning certain actions and events around the 14th of June that went to, among others, Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the basis of this report it can be seen that it is a report bearing the date that you refer to, the 14th of June, 1993, that it's sent by Mr. Zarko Keza inter alia to Mr. Stojic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And to follow-up on Judge Antonetti's point, if we look at persons 4 and 5, and maybe you can assist us and maybe you can't. Isn't it correct, sir, that Mr. Domizat [phoen] was another senior officer in the Republic of Croatia armed forces and can you tell us why Mr. Domizat and why the Split operations zone Colonel Bonacan [phoen], Split being in the Republic of Croatia, why they would be being copied on the intelligence reports from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just give you the answer that I've already given to His Honour Judge Antonetti, that I will dot not know why it was sent to them. It's only the person who sent this can say why he did that. Anything else that I would say would be speculation, and I do not wish to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, look at item 6 of this document. Maybe we can find the answer there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've read this paragraph 6 now. That could be related to this letter, but I really don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry, I don't want to speculate, I don't know anything about it either; but it's interesting to look at paragraph 4, maybe there is a connection there why this letter was sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Take a look at point 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've looked at it. This para 4 or the issues related to para 4 confirm a situation that went on and on, and the problems that we encountered in the Croatian Community Herceg-Bosna regarding mobilisation, shirking from military duty, and desertions into the Republic of Croatia.
