So this para 4 makes sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to turn next very briefly to the topic of meetings at the Department of Defence, I might refer to them perhaps as section head meetings. I think they've been referred to in the purpose in these proceedings as the college. Do you know the meetings that I'm talking about, the meetings that would take place among the managers, if you will, within the Department of Defence that have been mentioned several times?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand what you are driving at. That's what I have emphasised so far in my evidence, and the transcripts presented here in the courtroom confirm that these were, indeed, college meetings of the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. My only further question on that topic, unless the Judges have questions, just to be clear, and when these meetings were being held and conducted, was it generally the case, perhaps with exception, that those meetings were chaired or conducted by Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure, but I believe the greatest number of those meetings were chaired by Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You recall an instance in -- later in 1993 where Mr. Stojic made it a point that he expected the head of the Main Staff to attend those meetings also on a regular basis, essentially ordered whoever it was at the time, Mr. Praljak or Mr. Petkovic to always attend those meetings? Does that ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would put it quite differently. College -- the college of the Defence Department consisted of heads of sectors, and they were represented by heads of certain administrations and representatives of the Main Staff because yesterday we had --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I apologise that I cut you off, we'll come to the documents in good time assuming we can get there. Is it correct, sir, that -- hopefully you'll be able to confirm this to me without the need to go back through the interview, but can you confirm, sir, that you were not involved in and really knew nothing about the funding of the Department of Defence? You weren't involved in that. You don't know where the funds came from. You just simply can't assist us on that topic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the answer I gave you during the interview five and a half years ago, or is it a new question now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir. You told me, and I'll just tell you, it can be found on part 2, page 12 of the interview; part 3, page 32 of the interview; part 2, page 13 of the interview. On several occasions, sir, you assured me that you knew nothing about the funding of the Ministry of Defence. You didn't know what the source of funds were. You simply could provide no information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, perhaps my learned friend can assist and point out to which part of examination-in-chief does this question relate to? It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've spent days talking about the Department of Defence, and its operations as deputy minister, I think while we have this here, it's information that the Chamber should have. The Chamber can reach its own conclusions about the operations of the department, if the deputy minister say that is he doesn't know where the funds came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll leave it to Your Honours, of course, but certainly I missed any reference in examination-in-chief to the issue of funding. But Your Honour, I will say no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: One question, Your Honour. Did you know anything about -- can you condition firm to us that you don't really know anything about the funning of the department of defence. That's the one question I asked that can be answered very easily. Yes, no, maybe, I don't know, to quote Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please put to me an exact specific question and quote my answer from that interview to avoid speculation on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm asking you the question now. Can you tell these judges, you are sitting here under oath, do you know anything about the funding of the Department of Defence during the period of August 1992, to November 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know my learned friend very kindly intimated that there was only one question on this topic. However, the number of questions is really a secondary issue. I would ask that my principal query - in fact, it is an objection - be ruled upon. This topic was not touched upon at all in examination-in-chief, and I would, therefore, ask why is it relevant to be raised in cross-examination. It doesn't arise out of examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, the issue wasn't raised during the examination-in-chief, what is your position? My position is well known to everybody, but what is yours?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't want to use the time to go into it. If the Chamber is not interested in it, then I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll turn to my colleagues from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, the Chamber will allow the question. Go ahead. Even though the issue wasn't addressed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I just say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What would you like to say? Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Precisely because of your goodwill and that of the entire Chamber, I would like to repeat that I'm a witness of the justice. I spoke to Mr. Scott as a suspect. At that time, Mr. Scott told me that anything I say may be used against me and against anyone else. As a legalist who in addition to five -- in spite of five prior telephone calls and other invitations refused to talk to them when the summons came, I came for that interview. I know about my rights. I knew that I could see Mr. Scott at that time, give him my personal details and defend myself with silence, without answering a single question. Instead I stayed for three days and answered every question that Mr. Scott put to me. Now Mr. Scott is taking me five and a half years back. I repeat, he never gave me a copy of the transcript in Croatian that he had promised when we finished that interview, and now I'm supposed to recall what I said or did not say on that occasion. And on the other hand, I'm a visual type. I prefer to see before I comment rather than hear. I really don't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, we have taken note of what you've just said. You were a lawyer, you were a judge once just like us; you are almost a colleague, and you know better than anybody else the scope of what you are saying. Mr. Scott has asked a question about the funding. It has nothing to do with what you said five years ago. Now you are a witness of this court. This a simple question Mr. Scott is asking, please provide an answer to this simple question. After its discussion, the Trial Chamber has decided that Mr. Scott will be allowed to ask his question. Mr. Scott, please ask your question and we hope the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you know anything about the funding of the Department of Defence during the time that you were deputy minister from -- deputy head during the time from -- well, unofficially, from September 1992 until November 1993, which then became official on the 15th of January, 1993. During that time-period, sir, can you provide the Judges with any information about the sources of funding and the funding -- the financial operations of the Department of Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be precise, but as far as I can remember, for the most part, we were financed from the estimated budget of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and as to any other sources of finance, I do not know. Do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you involved with --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry. I apologise to my learned friend. Your Honours, I wanted to let the witness answer. I have no problem with that, and I don't want to object. But I want this on the record. You made a decision, Your Honours, to allow the Prosecutor to ask questions beyond the scope of examination-in-chief. I want it to be on record that the Defence has almost never been allowed to do that. I want it on record that this right belongs to both parties and I, I'm speaking only in my own name, I feel threatened by the difference in approach. Your Honours, I do not want to comment on this. I feel frustrated about this decision, and I want it to be on record. I have nothing further to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, the Judges have deliberated as you could see and the Judges felt -- I did not develop the whole deliberation, we are not going to issue very long oral decisions given the fact that the accused are complaining about the duration of this trial - rightly so - I did not develop of course the contents of our discussions, but we discussed the issue of credibility, and we thought that in that discussion there might be an aspect related to the credibility of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I appreciate your position. I just wanted my position on record. But if authenticity is in issue and be credibility is an issue, then the witness should have been shown what he had said before, only then would his answer have been valid. We did talk about fairness, but it is true that sometimes there is no equality of arms between the parties. I wanted to rise and to say this because I want to be able to invoke this example when I have further questions that are important. I know that I was, myself, cautioned several times to state exactly the question from direct examination that my question has to do with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to move on because I don't want to take the time on it given where we are. I would -- if Your Honours felt it necessary at some point can respond to counsel's comments and give you my perspective, but not when we have the witness on the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that you knew Mr. Mate Boban before the war? You had known him before the war and had dealings with him from time to time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true that I had contacts from time to time. I said I knew Mr. Mate Boban as a person who was managing a commercial company in Imatsko [phoen] while my father held a similar job. And I personally first met him in the 1980s concerning a project in Siroki Brijeg. I had no contact with Mr. Boban before that, and I didn't know him personally before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go directly to, again, the period that I've mentioned several times today, roughly August 1992 to December 1993, during the core period of your involvement at the Department of Defence in connection with Mr. Stojic and shortly thereafter. During that time-period, sir, and again just so the record and you can hopefully be very clear, I'll state the dates again, between August of 1992 and continuing to December of 1993, can you tell the Judges approximately how many occasions did you have any conversation or meeting with Mr. Boban? And all I'm asking for now is a number or not al all, zero, not at all, two times, five times, how many times?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you meant zero to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How many times, sir, from August 1992 to December 1993, how many times during that period did you have conversation or meet with Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say I ever had any conversations with Mr. Boban. I was present perhaps three or four times, maybe five in that period where Mr. Boban was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say you were present. Present at a dinner party? Present at some official function? In these three, four, or five times can you tell us a bit more about the nature of those contacts?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I tried to recall, and in my proofing until I saw the record of the session of the HVO HZ-HB of the 17th May, 1993, when Mr. Mate Boban got involved. If you had asked me before seeing that whether I had been there in his presence, I would have said no, but I can't say that those were contacts or regular meetings or individual encounters. I repeat, how I recalled that meeting when Mr. Boban attended that meeting of the HVO HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We know about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let me try and help you. This is an important question that the Prosecutor is asking for himself and for the Judges as well, as well as for the Defence because there's a lot at stake here. Why, I'll be very clear and transparent, I have nothing to hide, we are trying via the witnesses and through the documents, we are trying to determine how Mr. Boban, Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, and yourself were working, were operating. If, Mr. Boban was meeting everybody, every day, during meetings, this would have a specific meaning, if he met somebody very rarely, this would have another meaning. So you just told us that you met him three or four times. Did you meet him in working sessions, at dinners, during receptions organised when somebody was leaving, at burials? This is very important for us to know. Do you understand the significance of this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand the question, Your Honour. I said perhaps it was three, four, or five times, and I can expand by coming back to that meeting with the ambassadors of the European Union, some meetings that ended by representative of the UNPROFOR. But I never attended a meeting chaired by Mr. Boban where some decisions would have been made. And I didn't attend meetings of the presidency of the Croatian Community Herceg-Bosna or the presidency of the party. I didn't attend such meetings. I was present during the contacts that I listed because I in a way I was a link between representatives of the UNPROFOR who wanted sometimes to meet with Mr. Boban, and I stayed during the meeting sometimes as a person just listening to the conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your answer is very useful and specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, a similar question just to be very, very clear. Once again you've told news the last few days several times about the locations of the Department of Defence offices, where you and Mr. Stojic had your offices. At those particular locations, at those particular locations during this same period of time between August 1992 and December 1993, can you tell us, if you can recall, how many times did you ever see Mr. Boban come to those offices? You ran into him there, he came to a meeting, how many times did you see Mr. Boban physically present in the offices of the Department of Defence senior officials such as you and Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure about one encounter, and I told you as much when you interviewed me, when I met him in passing on the stairway, and I'm not sure about another encounter, whether it happened or not; but I know we passed each other on the staircase, or on the landing of our building. And I told you as much five and a half years ago, I recall that clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you have an approximate time-period? If you can help us, if you can't just say, I can't recall. But can you put any date, can you put any time-frame on that meeting Mr. Boban in the hallway?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that you insisted a lot on that kind of detail, how it all happened, but I can say that it all happened in the period after the attack of the Muslims against the HVO on the 9th of May. But whether it was on the 15th of May or the 17th or the 20th, in any case, it could be mid-May or the second half of May, and I believe that's the answer I gave you then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm moving on to another individual, Mr. Jadranko Prlic. It is correct that you knew him before August 1992. And you had known him in the 1970s in connection with his being a functionary in some political party or activity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not say that he was a party official. I don't know Mr. Jadranko Prlic because as I say I was a scout for many years and Mr. Prlic then worked in some youth organisations or led some such body. And I told you I knew Mr. Prlic because he was president of the executive council at the same time when I was mayor of Siroki Brijeg. And I knew that he deputy prime minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina because I was an MP in the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina. When I belonged to a group of MPs who succeeded in promoting the idea that a younger group of people should be allowed to take position --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- such as Mr. Bogic Bogicevic and deputy prime minister was Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that it was and has been your view that there was no one in the HVO government at that time who was more powerful than Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question, what do you mean more powerful?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall saying sir, in my quote in my opinion no one could have been more powerful because he was at president of the HVO government, part 2 of the interview page 42: "Question: Sir, was there anyone in the government, was there anyone in the HVO government who had more power and authority than Jadranko Prlic at that time? "Slobodan Bozic: In my opinion no one could have more power because he was the president of the HVO government." That's what you said in 2003 and is that still your answer today, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all I have to emphasise for the benefit of the Court that in the interpretation of my evidence there were at least six or seven occasions when my counsel intervened, and he knew initial very well. He intervened because of misinterpretations. I spoke knowing the position of Prlic's head of the HVO HZ-HB. And I'm speaking as a lawyer in view of the decision governing the temporary authorities. It was quite clear what the president's position was. That was Mr. Prlic. It would be quite different if I spoke about the most influential position that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, excuse me, you've' just said after complaining about interpretation and errors, you've just confirmed what did you in fact say, and you said that and tell me again I'm going to give you another chance: "In my opinion no one could have more power because he was the president of the HVO government." And my specific question to you again was, was there anyone in the HVO government who had more power and authority than Jadranko Prlic at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness answers, I think it's only fair to look at page 42 of the interview. My learned friend very properly puts the question. There's no dispute about that. However, the preceding question is important when one is assessing the credibility of the witness and the context, my learned friend's previous question in the interview was:

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "Who was the second most powerful individual in Herceg-Bosna after Mate Boban?" And this witness's answer was, "No, I do not know. No I do not know. I cannot answer that question. I wouldn't be able to answer that question because that answer can be commented upon from different sides." Your Honour, that was the preceding question. I think it's only fair that the context be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, except that was not the question I put to the witness. My question was the one I put to the witness. If he is saying he didn't say those words, he can say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But let me put it to you this way, sir, we are in The Hague today on the 5th of February, 2009. And you are under oath. Is it your position, can you confirm to the Judges today that in 1993 there was no person in the HVO government more powerful than Mr. Prlic. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, at this point I will object. What does he mean by "more powerful"?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm using his own words, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At this point -- at this point, he said now we are in The Hague, now he is rephrasing the question, and the witness say what is more powerful? If you look at the statement. I've read the statement several times, you see that continuously Mr. Scott is trying to put words into the witnesses mouth in the way he asks leading questions during the interview. So what is more powerful. In what sense? He can ask, Can Prlic direct a member of the government to do X, Y, and Z; but what does he mean by more powerful? It has different meanings, in different places, and different times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, can you refine your question and develop what you mean by more powerful. According to you, the Prosecution, what does more powerful mean. Is it the power to appoint people, power on the civilian authority, power on the military authorities, power to negotiate international treaties? I don't know. Can you elaborate a little bit on this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, going back to the transcript. Sorry, Your Honour, I've got too many loose pages floating around. It's my apology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can help you, Mr. Scott, I helped the witness now I can help the Prosecution. Mr. Karnavas made -- had an objection because in the question you put --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. You understood that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I was looking for -- excuse me, Your Honour I apologise for cutting across. Your Honour, my apology. I do understand the question. I was simply trying to find the point in the transcript before giving a further answer because I have been accused so many times in the last ten minutes of somehow being unfair. I want to look exactly back at the words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well while this is happening, just for the record, I will be asking for redirect or re-cross or whatever this is, but I will be asking for an opportunity to go into this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In light of what Mr. Khan said, Your Honour, I'd like to go back. I'll simply read the question. I'll ask the witness if he wants to say something more, he can. If he wants to say, I didn't say that, he can. I'm going to go back and so we have this broader context.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The bottom of page 41 of part 2 of the interview. And since I was being so unfair, the question was this: "What was the role of Jadranko Prlic in formulating and carrying out the policies of Herceg-Bosna? "Slobodan Bozic: That's what I told you. There was an organisation of authority where Jadranko Prlic was president of government, and the government role was very clear. That was also regulated by the organisation of that government and also individual ministries within that government. "Ken Scott: Who was the -- who would you say was the second to most powerful individual in Herceg-Bosna after Mate Boban? "Slobodan Bozic: No, I do not know, I cannot answer that question. I wouldn't be able to answer that question because that answer can be commented from different sides. "Ken Scott: Was there anyone in the government, was there anyone in the HVO government who had more power and authority than Jadranko Prlic at that time? "Slobodan Bozic: In my opinion no one could have more power because he was the president of HVO government." Now, Mr. Bozic, is there anything about those answers that you want to change today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you've jogged my memory a bit. Obviously your question is now a lot broader for a simple reason, because you took a particular context out of this interview and you wanted to gear me towards the power and influence of Mr. Prlic. If I were to give you answers today, I would say the same thing, that in the then provisional government of the HZ-HB, again Mr. Jadranko Prlic was at the head. As for his powers and obligations, they were specifically regulated by the statutory decision on the establishment of this authority. At that time, I didn't use the word power. And today I would not use the word power, greater or lesser power. As a lawyer, I wish to explain that it is logical in a collegiate and collective organ such as the HZ-HB, there would be one person that is leading this collegiate and collective organ. I do not wish to speak of any kind of power today, as I didn't at that time. I'm just saying this as a lawyer in view of the documents that existed then if we can call them legislative regulations, that this matter had to do with. I was not thinking of power, and I do not think of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May I move on, Your Honour? Does the Court have any further questions on this matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to draw your attention now please to Mr. Bruno Stojic. As I understand it you had known Mr. Stojic before the war, during the time when you were, as you've told us, the chief of police and Mr. Stojic at the time was an assistant minister for Internal Affairs or interior; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During the time that you worked with Mr. Stojic as a deputy head of the Department of Defence, to your knowledge or was it ever expressed to you, that Mr. Stojic had any dissatisfaction with the way you performed your job?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beg your pardon. I didn't understand that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During the time that you worked with Mr. Stojic as a deputy head of the Department of Defence, to your knowledge or was it ever expressed to you that Mr. Stojic had any dissatisfaction with the way you performed your job?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. It is possible that something like that was the case, I'm not ruling out that possibility, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you consider throughout that period, sir, that you carried out your responsibilities and your functions at the Department of Defence including assisting Mr. Stojic to the best of your professional abilities, conducted yourself in a professional manner?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all right, this question is such that it is unpleasant to give an answer. I was supposed to speak about myself, what I was and what I wasn't. However, all my life --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. You don't have to be modest for the moment, I've asked a question. We are in the courtroom. It's a very simple question and very simple answer at least initially. Did you conduct, did you view that you conducted yourself to the best of your professional ability and conducted yourself in a professional manner. Yes or no? If you say no, I'll ask you why you would answer no, but let's start just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In every work that I do, I try to act professionally, responsibly, and in the framework of my expert knowledge; and I will not be the judge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, did you consider that it was your -- part of those professional duties and part of your desire to do the best job possible was to keep Mr. Stojic informed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we really have to go back to the basics of what it was that I did, and that was within the civilian sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... is there any information, sir; can you tell the Judges, do you recall any time you withheld information from Mr. Stojic, you said, Yeah, I just received this information, but I'm just not going to tell Mr. Stojic. Can you remember anything like that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this kind of situation did not occur, at least as far as I can remember at this particular moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You officed immediately across or adjacent to Mr. Stojic with a secretary there; correct, sir, that you sometimes met with Mr. Stojic as much as three or five times a day?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give a precise answer now. At any rate, we met as often as the situation required when we were together at the office. Now, was it twice or three times or more than that? We met when necessary and sometimes we wouldn't even meet a single time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, any instance in which you did not either failed or refused to carry out a task or assignment given to you by Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that I refused to carry out a task or assignment given to me by Mr. Stojic. At least now that I go back in time 17 years that is. I doubt that there was a situation when I would not carry out a task or assignment given to me by Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know how many times in your experience based on your position, Mr. Boban and Mr. Stojic would meet together?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that Mr. Boban was at our department once when I met him. I don't know whether he was there another time or not, but as for how many time Mrs. Stojic and Mr. Boban met and when, I really cannot speak about that because that would be speculation. At any rate, I know that they did meet, but how often that happened and where and when, I cannot say with any specificity. At any rate, I did know that they did meet depending on the need involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, staying with Mr. Stojic and his continuing involvement in some of these matters after he ceased being head of the Department of Defence, is it correct, sir, that the position that he took on immediately following being head of the Department of Defence was head of the office for production and trade of arms?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think, as far as I can remember from those times that there was a decision that was published in the Narodni list and I think you showed it to me when we discussed Mr. Stojic's positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's look at it briefly again, P 07461. P 07461 in the binder number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, again I must be missing something, but it's my recollection, and certainly it was I was reminded by Ms. Nozica, that the Prosecution didn't lead any evidence in its own case regarding the time when Mr. Stojic was head of the office for production and trade of arms. That being the case, this evidence was not led by my learned friend in the Prosecution's case in chief. I'm rather at a loss to see why now in the Defence case their seeking to elicit evidence on this issue that they chose not to lead when they had an opportunity to do so. So clarification in that regard would be most enlightening.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll connect it up, Your Honour, in another part of my cross-examination. With the witness in the room, I don't want to say the reasons I want the information at this point. I don't think I have to tell the witness that. Is there some point of controversy that the Chamber should not know what Mr. Stojic did after being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Witness, if Mr. Stojic, who was minister becomes the head of the department, the department of production and trade of arms, it's a bit surprising in the -- in the way countries operate in the European Union, when somebody is a minister, he doesn't become number 5, 6, or 8. So is it true as far as you know that Mr. Stojic after being minister became the -- an administrative officer; and if this is the case, is this normal? Is this abnormal? What is your position? You may have your own opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I see on this page of the Official Gazette, Mr. Stojic was appointed the same day of the head of the office for production, and I for the office of for cooperation with UNPROFOR. I have a position of my own in this regard. I can understand that you who come from states with an organised system and tradition, you find it quite incomprehensible that someone can come to the position called head of the department for production and manufacture of weapons. But I look at all of this as the time when there was this provisional functioning of authority in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And in that situation there are no rules like the rules prevailing in the west that you come from, that someone can come from this lofty position to a position is at a much lower level. I think that I've often said this to Mr. Scott as well when we talked, I personally viewed this as a time when one had to try to bring this war to an end as soon as possible, and that everything that we were doing was provisional, temporary. And from that point of view, we shouldn't really care about who was doing what and who held what particular position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I can ask you to next look, please, at P 10785 in binder number 2. P 10785.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is an issue of law that I'm going to be going into. I'm happy to deal with it now. It's the same objection as to one I raised earlier. This document relates to a period after November 1993 at a time when my client was in the personnel department. The Prosecution have given no notice at all in relation to this -- this is not an exhibit. It has not been led in the Prosecution's case in chief. No evidence at all, not a scintilla of evidence has been led in the Prosecution case in chief in relation to this matter. Your Honour, there is a real issue of notice here. Of course, it would go both to the inadequacy of the indictment, but, Your Honour, when looking at the sufficiently of notice, it's quite proper, and according to the case law of the Tribunal to look at the pre-trial brief and even to look at the Prosecution's case in chief and the facts that they have led. They have not brought any evidence in their case in chief, made no reference to this part of -- this portion of my client's occupation at any time prior to today. In those circumstances, it is completely inappropriate, in my respectful submission, and a misuse of cross-examination to raise issues that the Defence do not have proper notice are going to be inquired into. Your Honour, I do cite case law from the Rwanda Tribunal, it's the Prosecutor and Bagosora case number - excuse me ICTR 9841-T. And it's the decision on the request for severance of the three accused, 27th of March, 2006. And, Your Honour, at paragraph 7, the Trial Chamber, in that case, made it very clear, and it is, in my respect not remarkable. It is a common sense, logical position. And they had a cross-examination of Defence witnesses by the Prosecution must be defined and limited by the evidence presented during the Prosecution case. The Prosecution may adduce evidence during its cross-examination which corroborates or re-enforces evidence presented during the presentation of its case. But Your Honours, this is the critical bit that comes next, but they may not, at this stage, venture into new areas. This document is dated the 24th of May at 1995. This area of evidence has not been referenced at all in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, nor in the Prosecution's indictment, nor in any part of the Prosecution's case. To do so now in cross-examination is contrary - in my respectful submission - to the rules detailed by this court about due notice, and it's impermissible; and I would ask that Mr. Scott not be allowed to refer or put this document to the witness unless some proper grounds can be put forward justifying a departure from what I respectfully submit to be the very clear and non-controversial jurisprudence of this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Khan, with all due respect -- yes, Mr. Ibrisimovic, I was going to answer to Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I do apologise for interrupting you but I would just like to join Mr. Khan in saying what he was saying. And I would like to go back to your decision from the 27th of November. This document is not on the list, and the Prosecutor should explain to us what are these exceptional circumstances that make it necessary and justified to show the witness this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic, you are perfectly right, this document should have been -- the Prosecutor should have told us this document is not on the list 65 ter; so, therefore, I would like to the document to be filed. And you are right in that, Mr. Ibrisimovic. Come coming back to Mr. Khan. Mr. Khan, you presented your argument. You took five minutes. And listening to you, I was thinking about Mr. Coric's letter, about what Mr. Praljak told us a while ago, and what Mr. Stojic told us. And I thought, well we are just wasting five minutes on a document. And what does the document say, that Mr. Stojic in 1995 had position function. What is the interest of wasting time? It is true, of course, Mr. Stojic had a function at a position why is that prejudicial to Mr. Stojic's -- in 1995, he was responsible for personnel affairs. Secondly, is there -- this document, you know this document by definition. You are Mr. Stojic's counsel, so with Mr. Stojic you probably asked him, What did you do in 1990, 1980, 1995? What did you do at the time? What was your position? He probably said, I was this, I was that; so this document is not something you just discovered. This is what I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, allow me to however feebly to try to assist. I'm very happy on behalf of Mr. Stojic to make an offer on proof that on the 24th of May, 1995, my client was the assistant to the minister of personal affairs. That is not my objection. My objection is that as far as time is wasted, it's been wasted because the Prosecutor is seeking now that he chose not to do in the many years prior to today which is to lead evidence in the first time in relation to the period after my client was head of the Defence Department. They should be estopped from doing so. Your Honours, this will save time. The matters are quite clearly put by the Prosecution in the indictment. They were quite properly put in the pre-trial brief and in the Prosecution's case. And there was no reference at all to the period of time May 1995 and my client's work in the personnel department. That being the case, my objection is based - in the greatest of respect - on principle. Why open a door to new litigation in relation to matters that were not inquired by the Prosecution in the years that they had to present its evidence. The fact that they did not has some consequence. We don't have notice to investigate new vistas that the Prosecution now in its -- in our Defence case seeks to open up. And Your Honours, the case law I cited is exactly on point, is exactly on point, they should be prohibited now at this late stage opening up areas that were not opened up earlier. And Your Honours, I would ask for a ruling on this issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, may we simply say briefly, we support the application and we also specifically draw attention to Your Honours' own order of the 27th of November, 2008. Your Honours know that four of the accused are dissatisfied with that decision and have an appeal with Your Honour's certification on foot. But the decision as it stands, regardless of what happens on appeal, strongly supports Mr. Khan 's position. And just that the single point, Your Honour, that the question of prejudice may be an issue which then arises as part of the submissions and debate which will ensue if the Prosecution makes its application and presents the exceptional circumstances to Your Honours to justify the use of that exhibit and exploration of that area. But it's not the other way around. We don't have to argue the prejudice points and the prejudice issue in advance of the Prosecution complying with the order which Your Honours have clearly made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, why wasn't this document on the 65 ter list? And what is the usefulness of this document which shows that Mr. Stojic on the 25th of May, 1995, had a specific function? Could you please answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First of all, Your Honour, this is cross-examination. It directly relates to something that is not new. I will tell you that ultimately, I will attempt, I may fail; but it relates to something that happened in 1993 that this Chamber has heard extensive evidence about. No one has heard my question yet. No one has any idea to be perfectly honest where I'm going, maybe that's part of the problem, but to anticipate, not knowing, and object having no idea how this evidence might be applied is premature. There is no requirement in the Tribunal law, and I will hazard on this occasion to make a fairly categorical statement. There is no law that requires cross-examination material to be put on the 65 ter list or to be provided advance notice. As the Chamber knows from this case, there is never been a requirement for any party including the Defence to give advance notice of their cross-examination material. So much of the argument is simply based upon completely incorrect notions of law. Number one. Number two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I was turning to my colleague because we have issued a decision in this regard, if memory serves me right because the legal officer did not have the time to find the decision. Maybe she'll find it now, but I have a good memory, so I'll try. The Chamber at the time had decided that during the cross-examination the Prosecution could submit a document to a witness even if such document had not been included in the 65 ter list. But solely to check or to test the credibility of the witness, and the Trial Chamber had added, and again I'm just using my memory here, this document was not going to be admitted. This is in summary the content of the decision we had issued at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The decision we took on the 27th November regarded admission of documents, and it is the practice of this Chamber that documents not intended to be asked for admission can be put to a witness in cross-examination. Those are two entirely different questions as long as Mr. Scott does not want this document to be admitted. He can take it as a basis for questions to the witness. I'm not talking about now about the date of the document, but I think that is really the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this, in fact, on behalf of Mr. Stojic, the objection is not founded on the fact that this document is not on the Rule 65 ter list. That is not the objection. The objection is based upon the Bagosora case law, and as others, I've got a list of other cases, that the Prosecution should be estopped. They should not be permitted to go into new areas now in cross-examination to elicit evidence that they chose not to lead evidence about in their own case in chief. Your Honour, we didn't touch upon this issue in the case in chief, so my objection, I am not going to repeat it, was not predicated upon these two documents. 10784 and also this current document P 010783 not being on the Rule 65 ter list. Your Honours have made a ruling, no objections taken. It's simply the fact that the witness is being opened up to new areas that we haven't inquired into. The Prosecution, most importantly, have not given us notice were in dispute neither in the pre-trial brief or in the case in chief. Now to open up these new areas in the Defence case is inappropriate and that's exactly what the Trial Chamber, as I read out, in Bagosora decided. Your Honours, another case in Bagosora as well, I can read it from September 2006. Testimony which broadens the facts imputed to the accused or the nature of his culpability are inadmissible. But the main quote I relied upon was the decision of Bagosora of March 2006, and that was the basis of my objection not that fact that we didn't have notice on the 65 ter list. I hope that clarifies, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's exactly right and with respect Your Honour's recollection of your own order is not surprisingly [indiscernible]. But paragraph 4 just two brief citations from that order, the 27th of November; paragraph 4 of Your Honours's order: "According to the joint Defence, new documents as defined are those documents that were not admitted during the Prosecution case or during the Defence cases, whether or not they are on the 65 ter list of the Prosecution." The points that Mr. Khan has just made. And Your Honours, that was our definition in the motion, that although Your Honours didn't accept the motion, you did adopt that definition for working purposes. And then the key paragraph in the conclusion was paragraph 23: "In conclusion, the Chamber does not deem it necessary to adopt new guide-lines as the jurisprudence is sufficiently clear." But then Your Honour stated, "In principle all of the documents essential to a party's case must be tendered into evidence during the phase of the presentation of its case in chief." We are talking about the Prosecution here. Consequently, if after the conclusion of its case, and its case has concluded, the Prosecution seek toss tender, in quotes, "new documents." And Your Honours, didn't depart from our definition of that into evidence in order to establish the guilt of one or several accused, it must justify its request by providing exceptional reasons in the interest of justice to admit these documents. And that is not is what has happened. So Your Honour, we are, of course, very grateful and any support from previous cases is extremely valuable. But here the key issue is Your Honours's own order in this very case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, I think there may be some confusion, because I see Judge Trechsel shaking his head in agreement, in agreement, I think, in agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think the English language it would be nodding that would be as opposed to shaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right, right, nodding. And I guess maybe we need a point of clarification, whether if we intend to -- whether the document is intended to be introduced into evidence, whether there needs to be preclearance, as it were, whether you need to get permission to -- or whether, even if you don't intend to tender it into evidence, but merely using it whether you still need to get preclearance. I think that's the one objection, not the objection that was being raised by Mr. Khan. Mr. Khan's objection is much more not subtle, pretty blatant and different. But I think with the use of the document, it was my understanding, if I was going to use a document that was not on my list, I would first need to get authorisation, permission from the Trial Bench, and we did seek that authorisation throughout the course when we were putting on our evidence. Obviously the -- any party can use documents that are outside their list provided that they are relevant, but it was my understanding that we needed to get preclearance from the Trial Bench. Now, whether that is the exception -- that is only necessary when you intends to introduce it into evidence and have it be part of the evidence versus merely using it to confront a witness or to show it to a witness whether it's to refresh their memory or to impeach, I leave it up to the Court. But I don't know whether I've been helpful in any way in trying to figure out this conundrum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to have the break. Mr. Khan a moment ago was talking about the Bagosora case law. I would like to thank him for reminding us of such case law. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, I apologise to Mr. Khan. I am going to stand and interrupt at this point because we are back into the same syndrome that we were in, got in the other night. The Defence is allowed to continually pop up and down, go on, get the Chamber's attention, talk, talk, talk. I started my response. I what cut off and then we go on and on and on. And I do object to this procedure. I'm tired of being treated as an afterthought. It is unfair. I apologise to Mr. Khan and procedural aspects -- excuse me, Your Honour. I'm going to finish my comment, Your Honour, I'm going to finish my comment no matter who standing up. Because I'm the one that always keeps getting cut off. I want to say very clearly, Mr. Khan, I apologise for interrupting you, but this goes on all the time. And it just -- we just -- they just go on and we are cut off and we never come back. You're going to take a break and you're going to deliberate. Oh well, I wonder what the Prosecution thought. We should get equal time. We should get equal time. I want every minute, I want every minute that the Defence have gotten to deal with this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no objection. I don't mind for a moment my learned friend standing up. I don't mind for a moment, and no offence is taken. What I was going to propose, Your Honour, is, of course my learned friend was going to be granted time perhaps after the break. What I've identify' asked my legal assistant to do is bring up the Bagosora case and copies will be served upon Your Honours and also my learned friends of the Prosecution. You have the benefit of the short break, and then could respond in total to all the submissions put forward by the defence. And, of course, I do understand his predicament. It is extremely frustrating when there are six Defence counsel on their feet in a case of this type. That is one of the consequences of a multi- accused trial. Your Honours, what I was proposing is that the judgement in Bagosora, at least one of the judgements I referred to, there are many others; but one judgement be handed to Your Honours. It can be looked at by Mr. Scott my learned friends so that he is not prejudiced. And once have the benefit of looking at that decision, he can address the merits of my objection or otherwise. Your Honours, I wonder if that assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I was about to take the floor and you interrupted me, which is not proper. I gave you the floor. Of course, of course, you will be allowed to develop your answer to the objections raised by the Defence counsel. Indeed there are six accused, there are six Defence counsel who are -- who may raise objections. This is your own law. This is common law that governs these proceedings. In another system things would be different. Unfortunately these are some of the draw back backs of this system, and that's the reason why these proceeding are very lengthy. And this is what I will explain to Mr. Coric when I see him again. This is the problem, lawyers, Defence counsel take the floor rightly, wrongly, we don't know. But you have the possibility to react. However, in the current circumstances, and I can only agree with you, we had no idea what the question you were about to ask was. Before we heard the question, objections were raised. This was the problem. We didn't know what you were about to show, and some objections were raised by the Defence counsel based on various legal aspects which may be deserved some attention. This is the situation. Now, Mr. Scott, of course, you will be allowed to answer. Would you want to answer now or after the break it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I can just comment -- excuse me. If I can just responds to a couple of observations the Chamber has made or the Mr. President has made, and I'll reserve to address the merits of the Defence arguments in a moment. I do apologise for cutting across, Your Honour. I apologise for that. There is a sense of frustration when this seems to happen on a number of occasions when the Prosecution loses -- seems to lose the floor in mid-argument, in mid-submission and then not get if it back. I apologise, but I do apologise for cutting across to you. The Court has my apologies. I have no problem with the six accused all being able to -- of course there are six accused. And of course, I have no problem or objection -- I have no problem, of course. It's a matter of procedure with all six being able to say what they want to say. That's not the nature of -- that isn't the nature of my frustration. However, when I'm given the floor, and I stand up and then halfway through, not even somewhere into my submission, somebody else, the way I put it, pops up and all of a sudden I've lost the floor again, that's the part that I do object to. All six say as much as they want to say. I don't care. Give them a week to say it. Give them 60 hours. I'll sit here for 60 hours and I'll listen to it as long as we get the same amount of time in response. There has to be some rhyme or reason to the order of people getting up, popping up, and making their submissions. I apologise if any of that offends the Chamber. I'll be happy to address any further aspects of the pending issue following the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You will address those aspects after the break. Indeed you are right, when you have the floor and you were interrupted by somebody this is not pleasant. And I do understand that a moment ago when you were on your feet, the Defence counsel raised objections not knowing what you were about to say. I do subscribe to your point of view in this regard. And vise verse, of course, when the Defence counsel want to say something and the Prosecutor stands up, I would agree with the Defence and say, Yes let's hear what you have to say, and then we will see. But here again we will realise that it was much ado about nothing. Anyway, we'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll bring in the witness once Mr. Scott has developed his argument. Mr. Scott, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think my comments will be brief. I don't intend on this particular moment to get into a long discussion of jurisprudence. I think it's fair to say there may be parts of the Chamber's 27 November ruling that, of course, time will tell the exact nature and scope and the application of that ruling. And I can understand where it might take -- might take sometime and experience for all of us to come to terms with exactly how that rule will be applied. That is just simply as a prepatory comment. The basic, position, Your Honour, is that there's been a lot of speculation so far about what the document and the evidence may or may not ultimately relate to. It doesn't inject a new area into the case. It relates to something that there has been relatively extensive evidence in the case on during the Prosecution case in chief, and this witness, it's the Prosecution's position, there's an aspect that we submit, the Chamber may ultimately disagree, but we submit, connects this witness to that. As the Chamber has ruled previously, the fact that a document post-dates certain other events or even after the time-period of the indictment doesn't mean at all that it's not relevant to something that happened during that time-period. You may have had a document from 1995 as the Chamber has ruled on a number of occasions, has found it to nonetheless relevant to something that did happen in 1992, 1993. So that principle is a clear one, and as to that aspects of the date of the document, that is this is nothing new or different at all. As to the Mr. Khan's some of the language that Mr. Khan has quoted about from the Bagosora case, I will just without still, and I don't pretend to have studied and read all that during the break, but just to pick up with I'm not saying, I'm going to be very clear for the record, we are not saying this represents the core of our position. But picking up on part of the language, Mr. Khan says that it can't be a new area, but Prosecution can be allowed to corroborate and reinforce - I think that's the language I heard him say - evidence and issues that were part of the Prosecution case. If one wants to read it that way, I have no question that this evidence corroborates and reinforces something that is not new to the case or not opening a new area but it relates to something that has already been in the case clearly; and therefore, the Prosecution should be able to put it to the witness. Now, whether or not it's ultimately admitted or not that, of course as always, will be up to the Chamber, but the notion that there has to be a preclearance to parties cross-examination, prenotice, preclearance, pre-disclosure, preclearance; okay, you can cross-examine on that, I submit to Your Honours, is not what the law requires. And in try together administrate such a regime, it would be a nightmare. Because after every direct examination, there would have to be some of a series of disclosures and submission that would then go to the Chamber. And the Chamber would give some sort of a green light to the party about what cross-examination would be allowed. I don't think that is a workable system nor is it the jurisprudence. I put again the issue admission to one side. We are not there yet, if we tender it on our IC list or not we will see. If we tender it and the Chamber thinks it should not be admitted, I'm sure the Chamber will so rule, but we are not there yet. All we are try together do is cross-examine a witness on a matter that has already been this case, and it's our submission this witness is related to. That's all there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is, of course, not our contention that this is analogous to the various rulings on questions post-dating the period of the indictment, the decisions on joint criminal enterprise. It's fundamentally different, in our respectful submission, because the Prosecution clearly in its own case in chief, led evidence, led evidence out with the scope of the indictment; and it's position all along was consistent that this was relevant to cast light on the alleged criminality of that they were alleging in the context. Our objection is far more basic. It is simply that there was no reference at all, at any stage prior to today in relation to our client's functions and occupations whilst he was in the personnel department. Now, Your Honour, if my learned friend states that it corroborates or reinforces evidence presented during its own case, the matter can be very easily determined if my learned friend, I stand ready to be corrected, if my learned friend can point to that part of the Prosecution's evidence in its own case in chief where they led evidence relating to our client's functions when he was in the personnel department. If my learned friend cannot do that, it cannot be said now that a document upon which he proposes to rely corroborates, rather the distinction is clear, in our respectful submission. It amounts to opening a new door and a new area that the Defence have not had notice of, and may well not have investigated. So, Your Honours, that was the primary basis of my objection. It has nothing to do with the Rule 65 ter list. It has nothing to do with the analogy to JCE. It's to do in contradistinction to the ruling on joint criminal enterprise that the Prosecution hitherto has not led any evidence in relation to our clients's occupation and conduct whilst in the personnel department. Your Honour, it may well seem in abstract it was rather precipitous of me to stand and object before a question was asked. Your Honour, that may well be the case from one vantage point. However when my learned friend referred to an exhibit which in my submission, we take issue with, it is only proper for me to stand up and take issue with it, and give my learned friend a chance to show relevance. Your Honour, that not being the case, there is a standing objection that I would ask that the Trial Chamber rule upon. I'm most grateful, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just standing up again because it's not clear to me what further the Chamber wants me to do in terms of what particular question the Chamber might want. Mr. Khan seems to suggest that I have an answer to some question that would assist the Chamber. If I can assist the Chamber then certainly I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my learned friend Ms. Nozica points out there may be an error in the transcript that it doesn't signify when I started speaking. Your Honour, perhaps that can be corrected in due course: Your Honour, the second issue is as far as it assists my learned friend Mr. Scott, is the further clarification that we'd like is the reference to what part of the evidence in the Prosecution's case in chief where they led evidence on my client's work in the personnel department to show relevance. You can't corroborate that which has not been led at all. It's as simple as that. If I'm stand to be corrected, I'm ready to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the Chamber wants to hear it, I will go into it. I realise the witness is not in the room, but out of an abundance of caution I would ask to go into private session concerning it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in private session. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please forgive us because you were waiting outside. The break for you was probably a bit long, but there was a procedural issue we had to deal with, and we did so. Since we have very little time left and we have to stop at 1.45 sharp because there is another hearing after that I'm busy somewhere else in another trial, I just would like to tell you that we would have the opportunity to meet again next week on Monday at 2.15 p.m. that's what I wanted to say just to make sure at 144 minutes 55 seconds, we should not all of -- obviously we do not have enough time. Now that we have dealt with in administrative point, I would like to give the floor to Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, I think I was in the process of showing you two documents and let me just say again because I did not go back, I've not gone back to look at the transcript exactly where we left off before the procedural matters were raised; but I was simply asking you or trying to ask you a few questions about what you could tell the Judges about Mr. Stojic's continuing involvements with the department of Ministry of Defence after he was no longer the head or minister. I think we had successfully looked Exhibit P 07461 which confirmed again and there was confirmation from you in the courtroom there was no dispute that Mr. Stojic, on no longer being minister, was appointed head of the office for production and trade of arms and military equipment by a document, by an appointment of decision dated 22 December, 1993. I was then about to show you P 10785 in binder number 2. And if we can go there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I should say, Your Honour, not to embarrass the witness at all, I do understand because some of his eye problems that he has it very well may be that he has some additional trouble finding the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Scott, for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I've been impatient in that respect, I apologise. We'll try to assist you as much as I can, but at the same time the courtroom is extremely sensitive to time. Sir, if you can look at P 10785. Can you just confirm to us, please, that Mr. Stojic at some time in -- perhaps you can assist us, but at least as of the 24th of May, 1995, held a position that was described here in item number 1 in those of attendance it says: "Bruno Stojic, assistant to the minister for personnel affairs and chairman of the commission." I note that in the subject part of the document it says, "Meeting of the personnel commission of the Ministry of Defence." Can you just please tell us briefly about Mr. Stojic being assistant to the minister for personnel affairs and chair of the personnel commission when he took on those particular responsibilities and approximately how long he was in those positions, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, just a clarification of this title. Assistance to the minister for personnel affairs. I think there should be a pause, because the ministers - as I read this - the minister is the minister of defence. So it would perhaps be clearer if it read assistant for personnel to the minister of defence. Do I understand this correctly, Mr. Bozic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are right, Your Honour, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I also agree, Judge Trechsel. Thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you then just tell us, do you know approximately when Mr. Stojic took up these functions and approximately how long he continued in them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm seeing this document for the first time, but I can answer that it was in this period, whether it was a month before or longer before, I really don't know how long he remained in this position in personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If I can just press you a moment longer. You indicated earlier that you continued in these personnel administration functions, you said to the effect longer than you probably wanted to, possibly as late as 1995. Did you overlap, if you will, with Mr. Stojic in any of those functions related to personnel matters within Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I mean, when I left this acting position because I repeat, I was never officially appointed assistant for personnel affairs. I think Mr. Stojic came after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I think especially given the issues surrounding the document, I'll leave it at that for this juncture. Thank you, Your Honours, for allowing me to go to that. Sir, the last -- where we were sometime ago in going through a number of items in a few documents was I was asking you about your relationships or involvements with various persons, and we had been talking up until now or most recently about Mr. Stojic. I'd like to ask you very briefly a couple of questions about Mr. Coric. Is it correct that you had also known Mr. Coric for some time since at least 1989, 1990, and again the two of you had worked together either in the Ministry of Interior or when you were chief of police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Coric did not work at the Ministry of Interior the same time when I worked at the police, but we know each other from that period, 1989, 1990, but our acquaintanceship from that time does not have anything to do with my work with the police because he did not work at the police then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I may have misspoke, but thank you for your answer in any event. Can I just ask you, can you tell us when you were deputy minister, the way we've been describing it today of the Department of Defence and Mr. Coric was chief of military police, can you tell the Judges what interactions you had, the nature of the interactions that you had with Mr. Coric during that time within the Department of Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the work I did at the Defence Department, I explained to you already that I had no communication, no relationship with Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So the Judges can understand for purposes of this case and as Judge Antonetti said sometime ago they are trying to collect as much relevant information as possible, you don't really have anything to add, if I can put it this way, good or bad; you have no evidence to give concerning Mr. Coric; is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered your question in the same way as I answered yesterday to Mrs. Alaburic when I described my position at the Defence Department and the work that I did and which affairs exactly fell under my purview as deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me -- all right. Since we broached the topic, let me go a step further. When you had these department meetings or section head meetings or the college that was usually presided over by Mr. Stojic, was Mr. Coric one of the persons who attended as part of the Department of Defence structure?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Coric was one of the people who came to these meetings. Not all of them and not regularly, but he attended most of the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was the interaction, if any, between the personnel administration of the department in general of the HVO and the personnel administration as it related specifically to the military police? Did the section of personnel administration that was under your supervision, did that include personnel administration as it related to the military police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if my microphone is on. The personnel division, as I said yesterday responding to questions, practically prepared draft regulations, in fact, documents for Mr. Stojic concerning certain appointments so that when, under the decision of the internal organisation of the Defence Department, such a document was drafted, this document would go to the assistant for security for approval; and this document would go to the personnel division if the appointments were supposed to be made by Mr. Stojic in keeping with his authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me -- staying on this a bit longer than I forecast, so let me go back on that a bit. Sir, I don't think it's controverted at this point, the military police administration was part of the security section, if you will, section sector of the Department of Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, but I just wanted to explain to you the procedure how the personnel division would be involved in appointments within the Defence Department, that is appointments regarding the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And that then leads me to the next question, and since the personnel administration which you've supervised applied to the department as a whole, then it's correct, is it not, that that personnel administration was also responsible for the personnel administration aspects of the military police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The personnel administration practically processed all appointments that related to the Defence Department, following prior procedure, that is clearly specified in the decision on the internal organisation of the Defence Department, who is supposed to nominate whom, who gives approval, and who makes decisions. All these appointments since these were persons in the Defence Department are recorded in the personnel administration, and we could see yesterday from that document about the composition how many staff were recorded at the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did the records kept by the personnel administration department include, we've talked primarily about just now we are talking about appointments; but as part of the personnel file, if you will, did that also include disciplinary actions taken against members of the HVO or the removal of members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't dare give you a certain answer. I don't think so. I don't think all the disciplinary measures were recorded in their files, but it's very important to distinguish between different periods because the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is a problem, interpreters had difficulties following. Witness, could you please sit closer to the microphones and please try to speak louder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered this question put by Mr. Scott, but I'm not sure. I don't think the disciplinary measures were recorded in files, and I added that it's very important to know which period we are looking at, the period when the personnel division was formed in May 1992. Before the department, most of their job had to do with procurement, and it was only from the first half of 1993 that the personnel administration started to deal with affairs for which it was responsible according to its own organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, if I can just again stem on a bit longer then. I'm struggling a bit with the concept, I think most of us, I would hazard a guess, most of us would come from systems where if you were employed by or part of an organisation and you have a personnel file, if you will, kind of both the good and the bad is in the file. And if there's a poor performance record or disciplinary action or a soldier is disciplined for not keeping his weapon clean or he goes AWOL or whatever the action might be, wouldn't you want to find that -- wouldn't some subsequent officer perhaps want to find that in the personnel file of that soldier? Well, Mr. Praljak seems to be laughing, but I mean it as a serious question. Sir, there's no comprehensive personnel file at the HVO by which someone, a member of the HVO would have their personnel record? Are you saying that no such file existed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, the two of us had a three-day long conversation, and you asked me one of these questions comparing your very well organised state with the democratic system and very well organised services with something quite different. And I have to tell you again, we were working within temporary authorities dealing with things we were encountering for the first time. And I told you that the personnel administration started to define its own purview only in the first half of 1993 when ID cards were in preparation and when ID cards were prepared, these files then started to be filled in. And as for whether disciplinary measures were recorded or not, I told you I don't think so. Maybe to you, who come from a very well organised state, it seems inconceivable but I'm talking to you about realities. What happened in real life.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the few minutes that we have left, sir, if I can move on to another topic that we might be able to complete. Turning to the HVO Main Staff itself, is it correct, sir, that you never attended any meetings of the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a brief objection with your leave. If I remember correctly, in this courtroom we haven't seen a single record from the meeting of the Main Staff of the HVO, nor did a single witness speak about meetings of the Main Staff of the HVO. So I would only like the Prosecution to point out the factual foundation for this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, your objection is a waste of time. It's not because they may not -- may or may not be minutes that no informal meeting ever took place. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just again to be clear, sir, I'm again asking you in terms of what the assistance that you may or may not be able to provide to the Judges. You never attended anything that might be called a meeting of the HVO Main Staff. So you would not be able to provide to these judges any information about the workings of the Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. I did not attend any meetings of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, do you have any knowledge of how often or if at all, for example, during the time that Mr. Petkovic was head of the Main Staff, do you have any opportunity to observe Mr. Stojic and Mr. Petkovic meeting together or doing business, if you will; one as the head of the Main Staff and one as the minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I practically answered this question yesterday in response to a question from Mrs. Alaburic. I said that they met ad hoc depending on the situation, and we met on the same premises. As to the regular character of the meetings, I can't say they were regular. They were organised depending on the situation, if the situation so required.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bozic. Your Honour, that completes that small topic and without starting something new, I'd suggest that might be a time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Scott, you are right. You will address next week other topics. You've used, unless I'm mistaken, approximately 1 hour and 45 minutes. Very well. We will resume, as I indicated, our proceedings on Monday, Monday afternoon. Next week, we will be working afternoons. I wish everybody a good weekend, and we'll meet again on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
